subject: math

unit.title: Money: pounds and pence
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we use pounds and pence to pay and work out change?

title: Adding amounts and finding change
objectives: By the end, I can total a small shopping list and work out change by counting up.

vocabulary.definition: how much things cost all together
the price — what you must pay
the money the shopkeeper gives BACK when you pay too much
start at the price and count on to what you paid
the change rule written as a number sentence

emphasize: To find change, COUNT UP from the price to the money you gave — don't wrestle with taking away.
First hop to the next friendly ten, then hop to the pound.
Pre-empt subtracting the wrong way round (or thinking the shopkeeper keeps the extra).

keyConcepts: totalling two prices by counting on
change as the gap between price and payment
counting up via the next ten
misconceptions: the shopkeeper keeps the extra money — no change exists
counting the wrong direction or subtracting price-from-nothing (70 − 100, muddle)
totalling over the ten wrongly (30p + 25p = 50p or 65p)
counting coins by how many there are, not their value, when checking change
hooks: A pen costs 70p. You hand over a whole pound. Does the shopkeeper keep the extra — or give some back?
priorKnowledge: counting up to the next ten (number bonds)

human: a pretend shop: pen 70p, rubber 30p, ruler 25p, toy 65p — price labels on each
digital: number-line hop animations on the whiteboard block

delivery.humanNotes: You run the first ~8 minutes as the shopkeeper with REAL coins (hook + explain). Before the lesson: set up the pretend shop — pen 70p, rubber 30p, ruler 25p, toy 65p, labels visible — and have a £1 and £2 coin ready. Play it up: hold out your hand for payment. Keep the maths exact: total by counting on; change by counting UP from the price (65 → 70 is 5, 70 → 100 is 30). Lay real coins down for each hop. When you say the handoff line, the AI character takes over; keep the shop within reach — the child buys from it again during practice.

plan.goal: Pose the change mystery — does the shopkeeper keep the extra?; retrieve £1 = 100p.
plan.note: Let the child argue it out — don't resolve yet. The injustice of 'keeping the extra' is the hook.
plan.successCriteria: Child says the shopkeeper must give money back and recalls £1 = 100p.

script.say: Welcome to my shop! This pen costs 70p. You hand over a whole pound coin. Hmm… do I keep the extra — or give you some back? How much back, do you think? And quick memory check from last time: how many pence in £1?
script.adaptHints: Hold your hand out theatrically for the £1. Listen for '100p'; if shaky, count tens to 100 together before moving on.

humanHandoff.setup: The shop laid out with priced items (pen 70p, rubber 30p, ruler 25p, toy 65p); a £1 coin in the child's hand.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: Not yet — the human continues into the explain beat.

stuckProtocol: If £1 = 100p is shaky: drop pennies in tens into the pound pot again — 10, 20… 100 — before going on.

plan.goal: Model totalling (30p + 25p = 55p by counting on) and change by counting UP (65p toy, pay £1 → 35p).
plan.note: Lay a real coin down for each hop of the count-up: a 5p to reach 70, then 10p, 10p, 10p to reach 100. The coins on the table ARE the change.
plan.successCriteria: Child watches a full count-up 65 → 70 → 100 and hears 'the coins we laid down are the change: 35p'.

script.say: First, totalling. A rubber 30p and a ruler 25p — I count on: 30… 40, 50 — that's the 20 — then 5 more… 55. Total 55p. Now the mystery: CHANGE. This toy is 65p and you pay £1. I start at the price and count UP: 65 → 70 is 5p… 70 → 100 is 30p. 5 and 30 make 35p change. Counting up is much easier than taking away! — Now my friend on the screen will draw those hops. Watch!
script.adaptHints: Lay a coin for every hop and point at them when you say '35p'. Say the final sentence as written — it's the handoff.

humanHandoff.setup: The count-up coins (5p + 10p + 10p + 10p) still on the table next to the 65p toy.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: When the human says 'Watch!', the AI character starts the next beat.

plan.goal: Shared count-up: the pen (70p) paid with £1 — the child does the hops on a drawn number line.
plan.note: Bridge the coin hops to a pictorial number line: 70 → 100 in tens. The child counts aloud; confirm by re-counting 70, 80, 90, 100.
plan.successCriteria: Child counts 70 → 80 → 90 → 100 and states the change is 30p.

script.say: I drew the hops from the toy — see how we jumped to 70, then rode the tens to 100? Your turn with the pen. It costs 70p and you pay £1 — that's 100p. Start at 70 and count up with me: 80… 90… 100! How many pence did we hop altogether? That's your change!
script.adaptHints: If the child hesitates, hop with fingers: three hops of ten. Celebrate saying 'thirty' as three tens.

blocks.prompt: The pen costs 70p. You pay £1 (100p). Count up from 70 to 100 — how many pence change?

wrongAnswers.why: gave back the price — counted the wrong thing
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 70p stays in the till — we count what's LEFT between 70 and 100. Start at 70 and hop the tens with me.

wrongAnswers.why: added the price and the payment instead of finding the gap
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're not buying two things! Start AT the price, 70, and count up to what you paid, 100. How far is the hop?

wrongAnswers.why: over-hopped — counted 70 itself as a ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: The first ten lands on 80, not 70. Hop again out loud: 80, 90, 100 — how many hops?

plan.goal: Reveal whether the child can total over the ten AND find change independently.
plan.note: Two-part diagnostic from the script: totalling 30p + 25p, then change for the 70p pen. Probe: 'show me the count up.'
plan.successCriteria: Child totals 30p + 25p = 55p (tens first) and finds 30p change by counting up.

script.say: Shop test! Two questions. First: a rubber is 30p and a ruler is 25p — what's the total? … Second: the pen costs 70p, you pay £1 — what's your change? Show me the count up!
script.adaptHints: After a correct total, probe: 'How did you add the 25?' Listen for tens-then-ones (30 + 20 = 50, then 5).

blocks.explain: Add the tens first: 30 + 20 = 50. Then the 5: 55p.

check.question: Total 30p + 25p; then change for a 70p pen paid with £1.

wrongAnswers.why: dropped the 5 when adding over the ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Add in two goes: 30 + 20 first — then don't forget the 5 hiding in the 25!

wrongAnswers.why: miscounted the tens jump (30 + 25 muddled with 30 + 35)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Split the 25 into 20 and 5. 30 + 20 = ? Then add the 5.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the wrong direction — tried to take 100 from 70 or gave back the price
wrongAnswers.remedy: Start AT the price, 70, and count UP to 100 — how far is it? The gap is the change.

plan.goal: The child runs the shop: total two items, then give change from £1; once secure, change from £2.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. Encourage using the real shop and coins — required on a miss (CPA step down: lay a coin per hop).
plan.successCriteria: Child totals two prices and finds change from £1 correctly at least twice, including one two-step (total then change) problem.

script.say: Now YOU run the shop! I'll be the customer. Total my shopping, take my money, and count up my change — coin by coin if you like. Ready? First customer coming!
script.adaptHints: Frame purchases with the child's interests (comics, stickers, football cards). Never change the prices.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the count went the wrong direction' or 'the jump over the ten slipped.'
Go concrete: coins out, lay one for each hop from the price to the pound.
One hint: 'How far from the price to the pound?'
Re-ask with a 90p item paid with £1 (one hop), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the change rule in their own words; end on an earned success.
plan.note: Child-led recall — the character listens, doesn't lecture.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'count up from the price' (or their own words) and can name the first hop (to the next ten).

script.say: So — how do we work out change: count up or count back? … Count UP, from the price to what you paid. First hop to the friendly ten, then ride the tens. You counted up coin by coin instead of guessing — that's exactly how real shopkeepers do it.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: laying a coin per hop, totalling tens first, checking by re-counting.

block.prompt: A rubber costs 30p and a pencil costs 20p. What's the total in pence?

wrongAnswers.why: added the digits 3 + 2, dropping the tens — mixing count and value
wrongAnswers.remedy: These are TENS: 30 is three tens, 20 is two tens. Count them all in tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the coins (or digits), not the value
wrongAnswers.remedy: Thirty means three tens. Add two more tens and count: 30… 40, 50.

hints: Add the tens: 3 tens and 2 tens.

reteach.say: Prices add just like tens. Thirty is three tens, twenty is two tens — five tens all together: 50p. Count it: 30… 40, 50.

block.prompt: A toy costs 90p. You pay £1 (100p). Count up: 90 → 100 is…
block.explain: From 90, one hop of ten lands on 100. The gap is the change: 10p.

wrongAnswers.why: thinks the shopkeeper keeps the extra
wrongAnswers.remedy: You paid MORE than the price — the extra comes back to you. How far is it from 90 to 100?

wrongAnswers.why: gave back the price instead of the gap
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 90p pays for the toy. We count what's BETWEEN 90 and 100. Hop it: 90 → 100 is…?

hints: One hop to 100 — how big is the hop?

reteach.say: Change is the gap between the price and what you paid. Stand on 90, hop to 100 — that's one hop of ten. 10p change. The price stays in the till; the gap comes back to you.

block.prompt: A rubber costs 30p and a ruler costs 25p. What's the total in pence?

wrongAnswers.why: added the tens but dropped the 5
wrongAnswers.remedy: Split the 25: twenty and five. 30 + 20 = 50 — now where does the 5 go?

wrongAnswers.why: miscounted the tens over the jump
wrongAnswers.remedy: Slowly: 30 + 20 is…? Count it in tens: 30, 40, 50. Then just 5 more.

reteach.say: Add money in two friendly goes: tens first, then ones. 30 + 20 = 50… then the little 5 hops on: 55p. Tens first keeps everything tidy.

block.prompt: A toy costs 65p. You pay £1 (100p). Count up — how many pence change?

wrongAnswers.why: hopped to the wrong ten (65 → 70 counted as 10)
wrongAnswers.remedy: The first hop is small: 65 to 70 is only 5. THEN ride the tens: 70, 80, 90, 100.

wrongAnswers.why: counting coins not value when laying the change
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the VALUE as you lay each coin: 5… 15… 25… 35.

wrongAnswers.why: gave back the price
wrongAnswers.remedy: The price stays in the till! Count only the gap: from 65 up to 100.

hints: First hop: 65 → 70. How big is it?

reteach.say: Two-part hop: first to the friendly ten — 65 to 70 is 5. Then ride the tens — 70 to 100 is 30. Add the hops: 5 + 30 = 35p change.

block.prompt: Which is the RIGHT way to find change for a 70p pen paid with £1?
options: Start at 70 and count up to 100
Start at 100 and count up to 170
block.explain: Change is the gap between the price and what you paid — count up from the price to the payment.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Start at 70 and count up to 100

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of finding the gap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Adding tells you the cost of TWO things. Change is a gap — where does the counting start, at the price or at zero?

wrongAnswers.why: no concept of change returning
wrongAnswers.remedy: You gave 100p for a 70p pen — is that fair? The extra 30p belongs to… whom?

hints: Change = the gap between price and payment.
Start at the price. Count up.

reteach.say: Picture a bridge from the price to the money you handed over. Change is the length of that bridge. For 70p and £1: stand on 70, walk to 100 — three tens. 30p change.

block.prompt: You pay £1 each time. Match each price to its change.

wrongAnswers.why: gave back the price, not the gap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count up from 55: 55 → 60 is 5, 60 → 100 is 40. What's the gap altogether?

wrongAnswers.why: hopped past 100
wrongAnswers.remedy: From 95, how far to 100 exactly? Count: 96, 97, 98, 99, 100.

hints: Each pair should add up to 100.

reteach.say: Here's the secret checker: price and change always add to 100 — they're bond partners to £1! 70 + 30 = 100 ✓. 55 + 45 = 100 ✓. If a pair doesn't make 100, it's a wrong match.

block.prompt: You buy the rubber (30p) AND the ruler (25p) and pay £1. How many pence change?

wrongAnswers.why: found change for only one item — forgot to total first
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two things in the basket! First job: what do they cost TOGETHER? Then count up from that total.

wrongAnswers.why: answered the total instead of the change
wrongAnswers.remedy: 55p is the total — great first step! Now the second step: count up from 55 to 100.

hints: Step 1: total the basket. Step 2: count up to 100.

reteach.say: Shop problems have two jobs. Job one: total — 30 + 25 = 55p. Job two: change — count up from 55: to 60 is 5, to 100 is 40 more. 5 + 40 = 45p change. Always total BEFORE you count up.

block.prompt: Stretch! A book costs £1.20 and you pay £2. Count up — how many pence change?

wrongAnswers.why: counted up to the wrong pound (£1.20 → £1 backwards, or stopped early)
wrongAnswers.remedy: You paid £2 — that's 200p. Start at 120 and ride the tens: 130, 140… all the way to 200.

wrongAnswers.why: mixed £ and p — treated £2 as 300p or muddled the units
wrongAnswers.remedy: £2 is exactly 200p. From 120 to 200 — count the tens on your fingers.

hints: Count up in tens from 120 to 200 — how many hops?

reteach.say: Turn everything into pence first: £1.20 is 120p, £2 is 200p. Now it's a counting-up job like any other: 120… 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180, 190, 200. Eight hops of ten — 80p change.

block.prompt: Ava buys a 75p comic, pays £1, and says her change is 35p. Check by counting up — is she right? Explain.
block.sample: No — from 75, the hop to 80 is 5 and 80 to 100 is 20, so the change is 25p. She hopped a ten too far.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: No; counting up gives 25p (75 → 80 is 5, 80 → 100 is 20)

wrongAnswers.why: repeated the over-hop instead of checking
wrongAnswers.remedy: Do the count yourself, out loud: 75 → 80 is…? Then 80 → 100 is…? Add your hops.

wrongAnswers.why: mis-added the check sum — 75 + 35 is 110
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try the checker: does 75 + 35 really make 100? Count on from 75: 85, 95, 105… oops. What DOES pair with 75?

hints: Check: price + change must equal exactly 100.

reteach.say: Be the change detective: price + change must make exactly 100. Ava's claim: 75 + 35 — count on: 85, 95, 105. Past 100 — too much! The true gap: 75 → 80 is 5, 80 → 100 is 20. 25p. Counting up catches every slip.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave totalling and change items (the child must decide which job is needed).
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach laying a REAL coin for each hop (CPA step down), then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one total-over-the-ten and one change-from-£1 by counting up → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'totalling and change'.
struggleProtocol: Name why (wrong direction / over-the-ten slip / forgot to total first).
Go concrete: coins out — lay one per hop from the price to the pound.
One hint: 'How far from the price to the pound?'
Re-ask with a 90p item from £1 (one hop), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: The shop sells whatever the learner loves (comics, dinosaur toys, football cards) — swap the items, never the prices. Keep 'you're the shopkeeper' role-play in the framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with an item the child can win (drop to a one-hop change if needed), then specific process praise: what they DID (counted up, hopped to the ten first, checked price + change = 100) — never 'you're so clever'.

differentiation.support: Count up coin by coin from the price, laying a real coin per hop; pre-total the first item; stick to change from £1 with one-hop gaps (90p, 95p).
differentiation.stretch: Two items and change from £2; 'what if you paid with the fewest coins?'; be the shopkeeper for the tutor and CHECK the tutor's (sometimes wrong) change.

extension: Full shopkeeper swap: the child sets prices for three toys, the tutor buys two and pays £2 — the child totals, gives change, and proves it with the price + change checker.
assessmentEvidence: Child totals two amounts (crossing a ten) and finds correct change from £1 by counting up, explaining the hops.
revisitLater: Money word problems return in Lesson 27 and Unit 8; use 'change from £1' as a retrieval starter within two weeks; the count-up strategy feeds subtraction by counting on.
